parts.text:
5
The following trace is seen on the screen of a cathode-ray oscilloscope.
The setting of the time-base is then changed from 10 ms cm–1 to 20 ms cm–1 and the Y-plate
sensitivity remains constant.
Which trace is now seen on the screen?
A
B
C
D

hints: Notice the x-axis is time: $10 \text{ ms cm}^{-1}$ means each $1 \text{ cm}$ horizontally equals $10 \text{ ms}$ of the signal.
Connect doubling to $20 \text{ ms cm}^{-1}$ to the spot speed: the same $30 \text{ ms}$ period now needs fewer cm, so the wave is squeezed horizontally.
Check the y-axis next: Y-plate sensitivity is constant, so the peak height in cm must not change, only the number of cycles across the screen changes.
walkthrough: Count the original trace: about 2 full cycles fill the roughly $6 \text{ cm}$ screen width, so one period is about $3 \text{ cm}$ wide.
Use $T = \text{width} \times \text{time-base}$: $T \approx 3 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ ms cm}^{-1} = 30 \text{ ms}$, and this real period does not change when the controls change.
Apply the new time-base: new width $= T / \text{time-base} = 30 \text{ ms} / 20 \text{ ms cm}^{-1} = 1.5 \text{ cm}$ per cycle, half the old width.
Keep amplitude fixed because Y-plate sensitivity is unchanged, so vertical peak-to-trough height in cm stays the same.
Therefore the same signal appears horizontally compressed by factor 2, giving about 4 same-height cycles in the screen width. This is option C.

A.explanation: Amplitude is larger vertically than the original trace, but Y-plate sensitivity is unchanged so peak height in cm must stay the same.

B.explanation: Only about one cycle is shown with reduced height, which would need a longer period and lower voltage, not a larger $\text{ms cm}^{-1}$ time-base.

C.explanation: Horizontal length of each cycle halves from about $3 \text{ cm}$ to about $1.5 \text{ cm}$ while vertical height is unchanged, so twice as many identical-height cycles fit on screen.

D.explanation: Only about one cycle is shown with larger height, which would need a longer period and larger voltage, opposite to constant amplitude and compressed time axis.
